chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Khalid ibn Jarir, from Abu al-Rabi' al-Shami, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
An oath is not valid for making permissible what is forbidden, nor for forbidding what is permissible, nor for severing family ties.

key_terms.تَحْرِيم: Making forbidden (tahrim); declaring something haram, the opposite of tahlil
key_terms.تَحْلِيل: Making permissible (tahlil); declaring something halal, the opposite of tahrim
key_terms.قَطِيعَة الرَّحِم: Severing family ties (qati'at al-rahim); one of the major sins in Islam, the opposite of silat al-rahim
key_terms.يَمِين: Oath/sworn statement (yamin); in Islamic law, a binding verbal commitment sworn by God's name

ai.seo_question: Is an oath to sever family ties or to change what is halal or haram valid in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a foundational legal principle: oaths cannot be used to override divine law. This ruling addresses a potentially grave misuse of the institution of oaths (yamin) — attempting to legitimize forbidden acts or prohibit permitted ones through a sworn commitment. The ruling also protects the sanctity of family ties (silat al-rahim), which the Quran and hadith tradition consistently elevate as a religious obligation.
